title: A great ball of stars
caption: The globular cluster NGC 1806, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Hubble's sharp view turns NGC 1806 into a sparkling ball of tens of thousands of stars, all bound together by gravity. Clusters like this are called globular clusters, and most are very old, having formed long ago, when the cosmos was far younger than it is now.

NGC 1806 is not in our galaxy. It lies in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a satellite of the Milky Way, and appears in the constellation of Dorado, the dolphin-fish, which is best seen from Earth's southern hemisphere.

The British astronomer John Herschel discovered it in 1836. He had traveled to South Africa to catalog objects best seen from southern latitudes, completing work begun by his father, William, who coined the term globular cluster. That same year, Charles Darwin visited him when HMS Beagle stopped at Cape Town, and Darwin later called Herschel one of "our greatest philosophers". Herschel also contributed to photography.

understand.summary: The image comes from the Wide Field Channel of Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys. A blue filter (F435W) is shown in blue, a yellow filter (F555W) in green and a near-infrared filter (F814W) in red.
understand.eye: Near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, and Hubble picks out individual stars in a cluster that lies in another galaxy.

behind.exposure: Not published on the source page.
behind.technique: Not stated by the source (single frame, stack, mosaic or panorama unknown).

explore: Exposure times were 770, 720 and 688 seconds, and the frame covers 3.1 by 1.9 arcminutes of sky. John Herschel scanned the sky with a large telescope and noted objects of interest, NGC 1806 among them.
alt: A dense, sparkling ball of stars.
